title: Close a hazardous-waste jug at the end of the day: funnel out and onto its drip tray, screw cap back on
instruction: You're done adding waste for today. Tidy up the waste station.
context: Chemical technicians, lab assistants and research staff add liquid waste to collection jugs every day (O*NET 19-4031.00, Chemical Technicians; 19-4021.00, Biological Technicians). EPA rules for satellite accumulation areas (40 CFR 262.15(a)(4)) say a hazardous waste container stays closed except while waste is being added. A funnel left standing in the jug's neck counts as an open container, and it is one of the most common violations inspectors cite. Open jugs let solvent vapor into the lab and can spill if knocked. At the end of the day the funnel comes out and goes on its drip tray, since it still holds residue, and the cap goes back on. A cap set on top of the funnel doesn't close anything. The instruction says none of this.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A black secondary-containment tray, 17 cm square and 3 cm tall, is fixed on the table at x 32, y -6. In it stands a fixed white HDPE waste jug (about 1.5 L): an 11 cm square body, 11.5 cm tall, with a carry handle on its back corner and a yellow hazardous-waste label with a red band on the face toward the arms. Its round neck is 3.2 cm across and 2 cm tall, open at the top 13.5 cm above the table, with a 2.4 cm bore. A gray polypropylene funnel (60 g) stands in the neck: an 8 cm cone, 4.5 cm tall, on a 1.4 cm stem 1.8 cm long, resting on the rim, with a molded grip tab (3 x 2.5 x 2.5 cm) sticking out toward the arms. The jug's red screw cap (5.2 cm across, 2.5 cm tall, 40 g) stands open side down on the bench at x 21.5, y -20. A blue drip tray (15 x 14 cm inside, 1.5 cm walls) is fixed at x 34.5, y -22.5, with a steel funnel holder in its middle: a ring 3.4 cm across with a 2.4 cm hole, 5 cm above the table, on a post.
scoring: Scored at the end. The funnel counts as still in the jug while its base is within 2.5 cm of the neck's axis and less than 3 cm above the neck's top. The cap counts as on when it is centered on the neck within 9 mm, its top rests on the rim (height within 4 mm), it is upright within 10 degrees and still. The funnel counts as on the drip tray when it rests seated in the holder (within 8 mm of the ring's axis and 6 mm of its seated height, upright within 20 degrees) or lies on the tray's floor with its whole outline inside the tray's walls. It counts as on the bench when it rests on the bare table top, not over either tray. A part still held by a closed gripper counts as none of these. The score is 0 while the funnel is still in the jug, whatever else, so a cap set on top of the funnel scores 0. Otherwise it is 1.0 with the cap on and the funnel on the drip tray, 0.5 with the cap on and the funnel on the bench, 0.25 with the funnel on the drip tray and the cap not on, and 0 otherwise, including a funnel knocked off the table or draped over a tray's wall. Both arms must also be back where they started (each tool point within 3 cm) and still, so the workspace is clear for the next person or job. The job done with the arms elsewhere scores 0.9. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, look at the neck and the drip tray at the end and try to lift the cap straight off.
reset_notes: Stand the funnel back in the jug's neck with its tab toward the arms, and set the cap open side down at its start mark. In a real trial the jug is empty or holds water.
fidelity: Close to real size. The jug and trays are fixed. The funnel and cap are rigid props that collide as simple blocks, with the neck, the cap's skirt and the holder built as square rings so parts really fit over and into each other. The cap is set down on the neck, not screwed: a seated cap counts as closed. No liquid or vapor is simulated. The funnel's grip tab is larger than on most real funnels.
